body.translated_text: why, disregarding the auspicious invocation (<s>maṅgalācaraṇa</s>), was the description of the rainy season beginning with "the sky having been covered" [GhKh.1] placed first? To this he replies: Now, having heard the <s>siddhāntin</s>'s (proponent's) question "What is the purpose of the auspicious invocation?", the <s>vādin</s> (opponent) says: The auspicious invocation is for the purpose of completing the treatise, preceded by the destruction of obstacles. Then the <s>siddhāntin</s> says: Is completion of the treatise preceded by destruction of obstacles [achieved] from the auspicious invocation alone, or from something else too? If the first alternative, then: is it that wherever there is an auspicious invocation, there is completion preceded by destruction of obstacles; or wherever there is completion preceded by destruction of obstacles, there is an auspicious invocation? The first [sub-alternative] has no proof: because even though there is an auspicious invocation in the <s>Kiraṇāvallī</s> and the like, non-completion is observed. Since that is untenable, neither is the second: because even though in the <s>Kādambarī</s> and the like there is completion preceded by destruction of obstacles, there is no auspicious invocation at its commencement. Therefore, since the auspicious invocation has no fixed connection with the treatise's completion — as for what you have said, that "an auspicious invocation must be made at the beginning, middle, [and end] of a treatise — for what purpose?" etc.

body.translated_text: I shall demonstrate that all this amounts to your lack of authority. For no wise person, having become authoritative, would disregard an auspicious invocation appropriate at the commencement of a treatise, since the learned have made it customary at the beginning of treatises. The auspicious invocation is threefold: in the form of obeisance (<s>namaskriyā</s>), indication of subject matter (<s>vastunirdeśa</s>), and benediction (<s>āśīḥ</s>). From among these, the auspicious invocation in the form of indication of subject matter — namely, the covering of the sky by clouds — has indeed been made. So there is no fault. As for the alternative "or from something else too" — since it is disregarded by poets, and since its applicability is seen [to follow] from the all-pervading rule [that the maṅgala secures completion]. In the <s>Kiraṇāvallī</s> and the like, however, the non-completion of the treatise is due to the abundance of obstacles and the scarcity of the auspicious invocation.

body.translated_text: Because by the maxim "as long as there is an auspicious invocation, so long is there absence of obstacles." And in the <s>Kādambarī</s> and the like, because the auspicious invocation was made outside the treatise [proper], and because of the scarcity of obstacles, there is completion.

body.translated_text: <s>Oṃ</s>. [Verse 1:] "The sky, reached by clouds — which rain down as if tearing the heart of a woman bereft of her beloved — dust on the earth is destroyed by waters, and neither the sun nor the moon is discernible." || 1 || "The speech of the woman whose lover is abroad is uttered" — thus the connection with the sixth [verse]. "This — what?" — "O you whose teeth are like jasmine buds" — thus connected from the second. '<s>salilaiḥ</s>' means 'by waters'; '<s>kṣitau</s>' means 'on the earth'; '<s>rajaḥ</s>' means 'dust'; '<s>nihataṃ</s>' means 'pacified, calmed.' Because the agent is in the instrumental case, the object is presented in the nominative — [this is] a verbal derivative construction. The locative '<s>kṣitau</s>' is used in the sense of location. '<s>Rajaḥ</s>' [means] the quality of <s>rajas</s>, dust, pollen, and also menstruation — [according to] the <s>Viśva</s> [lexicon]. Having done what was it calmed? — '<s>kham</s>' means 'sky'; '<s>upetya</s>' means 'having reached.' '<s>kham ākāśam udāhṛtam</s>' — thus in the <s>Ekākṣarī</s> [dictionary]. When the clouds reach the sky, then water becomes capable of calming the dust. Therefore '<s>kham upetya</s>' is said. Or — '<s>kṛtiyogaḥ</s>'

What kind of sky? — '<s>nīraṃ dadātīti nīradāḥ</s>' — those that give water are clouds (<s>nīrada</s>); '<s>nicitam</s>' means 'covered' by them. What kind of clouds? — '<s>priyeṇa hīnā yā strī</s>' — a woman who is bereft of her beloved; her heart itself is the earth (<s>avanī</s>); '<s>radayanti</s>' means 'they tear, they torment.' '<s>Rada</s>' [means] scratching. '<s>Api</s>' [indicates] certainty. '<s>Raviś ca candraś ca, tau ravicandrau</s>' — sun and moon; '<s>nopalakṣitau</s>' — not discerned, meaning 'gone out of sight.' O beloved! In such a time, how does he not come to me? — this is the sentiment.

body.translated_text: O dear one! <s>Niśi</s> means 'at night.' <s>Nabhas</s> means the sky. '<s>Nabhas</s>, <s>antarikṣa</s>, <s>gagana</s>' — [thus says] <s>Amarakośa</s> [1.2.1]. <s>Na bhāti</s> means 'does not shine.' '<s>Bhā</s>' [means] to shine [SV 272.8]. Here <s>niśi</s> is a locative in the sense of the object's circumstance. <s>Bhāti</s> is in the present tense. Since it is intransitive, only a nominative subject of neuter gender has been indicated. And intransitive [verbs] are stated [to be those] beginning with <s>lajjā</s> [SV 388.7-8]; from roots meaning 'to shine' [SV 388.8], [these are] intransitive roots.
